title: Executive presentations for CTOs
objectives: Structure an executive presentation around a decision
Design slides that support rather than replace the message
Deliver a concise recommendation with evidence

sources.title: Executive presentation and slide design guidance

verificationNotes: Presentation advice is general; adapt it to your organisation and audience.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
sections.body: An executive presentation is not a status report. It should state the decision needed, the recommendation, the evidence and the risks in the first minute. Everything else supports that. If the audience only hears the first two minutes, they should still know what you want and why.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Use a simple arc: context, problem, options, recommendation, cost and risk, decision needed. Keep each section short. Put detail in an appendix. Executives can ask for depth; they cannot recover time lost to unnecessary detail.

sections.heading: Slides as support
sections.body: One idea per slide. Use charts for comparisons, not decoration. Avoid dense tables. The slide should answer a question, not repeat your words. If a slide can be skipped without losing the message, remove it.

sections.heading: Questions and pushback
sections.body: Anticipate the three hardest questions and prepare answers. When challenged, acknowledge, answer directly and offer evidence. Do not defend a weak point; state the assumption and the test that would change it. End with a clear ask.

workedExample.title: CTO budget presentation (illustrative)
workedExample.body: Decision: approve 300,000 for platform engineering over two quarters. Recommendation: hire two engineers and replace legacy reporting. Evidence: current incident rate, cost per school, delivery lead time. Risk: hiring delay. Ask: approve budget and hiring now.

misconceptions: Detail should come before the recommendation.
Questions are attacks rather than information.
learn.explainTask: In 120 words or fewer, outline an executive presentation for a major technology decision.

knowledgeCheck.question: The first minute of an executive presentation should state:
knowledgeCheck.why: Executives need the decision and recommendation early.

knowledgeCheck.question: A good slide should:
knowledgeCheck.why: One idea per slide keeps focus.

knowledgeCheck.question: Detail belongs in:
knowledgeCheck.why: Keep the main flow short and put detail in the appendix.

knowledgeCheck.question: When challenged, a CTO should:
knowledgeCheck.why: Direct answers with evidence build trust.

build.business: Cretek leaders present technology decisions to executives and customers. Clear presentations improve decisions and trust.
build.problem: Build and deliver an executive presentation for a real technology decision, with slides, appendix and a Q&A plan.
requirements: State the decision and recommendation in the first minute
Prepare answers to three hard questions
Deliver a dry run and collect feedback
Produce slides with one idea per slide
constraints: Must be reproducible from the repository
build.design: Write a one-page presentation outline and slide list.
build.deliverable: Presentation slides, outline, Q&A plan and dry-run notes, referenced by path.

defend.scenario: The executive asks you to present a major technology decision in ten minutes.
prompts: What is the decision and recommendation?
What do you need from us today?

rubric.criterion: Decision and recommendation are clear early
Risks and reversal triggers are named
